claim: A written WotC house style guide does exist for the 5e era: 'D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing', Version 1.04a ©2013 Wizards of the Coast, distributed to freelancers/Adventurers League authors and later bundled on the DMs Guild; it governs mechanics of style, not prose voice.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing v1.04a (PDF, 9 pp.)
quote: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing

verdict.trueWording: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing
verdict.note: Page 1 title line reads exactly 'D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing'; footer on every page reads 'Version 1.04a (c)2013 Wizards of the Coast'; PDF is 9 pages, matching '9 pp.'. CAVEAT: the document itself says nothing about distribution to freelancers/Adventurers League authors or later DMs Guild bundling - that provenance is unverified by the source (only circumstantial: the host is adventurersleague.wordpress.com). Also 'governs mechanics of style, not prose voice' is nearly but not wholly true: a 'High Fantasy' section gives tone guidance (see index 8).

claim: The house style rests on the Chicago Manual of Style 16th ed. and Merriam-Webster's Collegiate 11th ed., with the guide covering only D&D-specific departures.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: The Chicago Manual of Style, 16th edition

verdict.trueWording: The Chicago Manual of Style, 16th edition
verdict.note: Page 1: 'We have two primary resources for the house style of DUNGEONS & DRAGONS products: The Chicago Manual of Style, 16th edition / Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary, 11th edition.' Minor overstatement in the claim: the guide says it focuses on matters 'where we depart from or expand on' those works, so 'only D&D-specific departures' understates the 'expand on' half. New Oxford American Dictionary is named as a third, backup resource.

claim: Rules text is written in the second person, which the guide presents as the standard way to achieve gender neutrality; singular 'they' is banned outside dialogue and 'he/she' alternation is forbidden.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: achieve gender neutrality by writing in the second person

verdict.trueWording: In rules text, we often achieve gender neutrality by writing in the second person.
verdict.note: Quote is a contiguous substring of the page-2 sentence. All three sub-claims confirmed: 'Don't use "they" or "their" as singular pronouns, except in an informal context like dialogue'; 'avoid "he/she" and "s/he" altogether'; 'don't alternate between "he" and "she"'. CAVEAT: the guide hedges with 'often', so 'presents as the standard way' is slightly stronger than the source.

claim: 5e inline subheads (heading 4) end in a period rather than the colon used in earlier editions, e.g. 'Keen Senses. You have proficiency...'
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon

verdict.trueWording: Contrary to past D&D usage, this subhead should be followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon.
verdict.note: Page 2 'Inline Subheads': 'The lowest level of our heading hierarchy is the inline subhead. It functions as our heading 4.' The correct/incorrect example pair is verbatim: 'Keen Senses. You have proficiency in the Perception skill.' vs 'Keen Senses: ...'. CAVEAT: the guide permits any terminal punctuation - 'Use a period, an exclamation point, or a question mark' - so 'end in a period' is narrower than the rule.

claim: Game quantities always take numerals ('3 hit points', '1 round', '30 feet') while narrative distances and durations follow Chicago and are spelled out ('fifty miles', 'six hours').
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: In rules writing, we use numerals more often.

verdict.trueWording: Numerals in Rules. In rules writing, we use numerals more often.
verdict.note: Every example in the claim is verbatim in the source: 'Anyone who touches the orb regains 3 hit points'; 'The spell lasts for 1 round'; 'The attack has a range of 30 feet'; and under 'But:' - 'The two cities are fifty miles apart' and 'After winning the fight, the characters slept for six hours.' The general rule cited is Chicago 9.2 (spell out zero to one hundred). 'always' is a shade stronger than the guide's framing but the substance holds.

claim: The guide fixes a verb list for mechanics: you 'make' a saving throw that 'succeeds or fails', attacks 'hit or miss', you 'deal' and 'take' damage, 'regain' hit points, and 'must succeed on' (not 'must make') a check.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: You make a saving throw, and it succeeds or fails.

verdict.trueWording: You make a saving throw, and it succeeds or fails.
verdict.note: Page 6 'Verb Usage' list carries all of it verbatim: 'You deal damage.' / 'You take damage.' / 'You regain hit points.' / 'You make an attack (or you attack), and your attack hits or misses (it doesn't succeed or fail).' CAVEAT on 'must succeed on (not must make)': the ban is conditional - 'Don't write, "You must make a DC 15 Strength check..." unless that sentence is immediately followed by a description of what happens on a success or failure.' Separately, for effects imposing a save the guide actually PREFERS 'the target must make a saving throw'.

claim: 5e abandoned the 3E/4E use of 'result' for the number rolled and 4E's 'save' for a successful saving throw; 'magic item' never 'magical item'; 'deals 10 fire damage' not 'points of damage'; 'hit point maximum' not 'maximum hit points'.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: We have abandoned that practice.

verdict.trueWording: We have abandoned that practice.
verdict.note: The sentence appears twice, verbatim, once for each abandonment: under 'Saving Throws' ('In 4E, we used "save" as a synonym for "successful saving throw." We have abandoned that practice.') and under '"Result" and Die Rolls' ('In 3E and 4E, the word "result" was sometimes used as a synonym for "the number rolled on a die." We have abandoned that practice.'). Also confirmed: '"magic item" and its variants should never be "magical item"'; 'write, "The spell deals 10 fire damage," not "The spell deals 10 points of fire damage"'; 'When you write about a creature's hit point maximum, avoid "maximum hit points."'

feature: capitalisation and italics of game terms
claim: Ability scores, class features, skills, planes, feats and 'Dungeon Master' are capitalised; spells and magic items are italicised and treated as titles, distinct from the effects they create.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: The italicized terms are treated as titles

verdict.trueWording: The italicized terms are treated as titles, even when they don't use title capitalization.
verdict.note: 'Terms to Capitalize' lists Ability scores, Armor Class, Artifacts, Class features, Difficulty Class, Dungeon Master, Feats, Languages, Planes of existence, Skills, Traits. 'Terms to Italicize' lists Artifacts, Magic items, Spells. The distinctness point is verbatim: 'Don't confuse one of these titles with an effect it creates... the wall of fire spell produces a wall of fire, not a wall of fire.' Note artifacts are BOTH capitalized and italicized.

claim: The only prose-tone guidance is a 'High Fantasy' paragraph: epic scope, teamwork over lone heroes, humour or tragedy permitted only if they would not seem out of place in Lord of the Rings or Game of Thrones.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: ring wraiths aren't used for gags

verdict.trueWording: there are moments of humor with the hobbits, but ring wraiths aren't used for gags
verdict.note: Quote is verbatim apart from the source's curly apostrophe in 'aren't'. The 'High Fantasy' section confirms epic scope ('the epic scope characteristic of that subgenre') and teamwork ('The lone knight fighting a dragon is less characteristic of D&D than an adventuring team fighting a dragon'). CAVEAT: the LotR/Game of Thrones test is framed as a 'When in doubt' heuristic, not the permission condition - the stated condition is that humor/tragedy be 'true to the facts of the brand and don't overtake the general tone'. 'The only prose-tone guidance' is the reviewer's inference, but it survives a read of all 9 pages: no other voice or register section exists.

claim: American spelling, serial comma required, possessive 's' after names ending in s ('Asmodeus's'), 'non-' hyphenated before fantasy races ('non-elf') but 'nonhuman', 'not' contractions encouraged, vertical lists introduced by a full sentence and colon.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: We require the serial comma.

verdict.trueWording: We require the serial comma.
verdict.note: All six sub-claims confirmed verbatim: 'We use American style for spelling and punctuation'; the serial-comma sentence; 'We write "Asmodeus's lair," not "Asmodeus' lair"'; 'non-elf, non-dwarf, non-orc, non-drow (but nonhuman, as in Webster's)'; 'We encourage the use of contractions formed with "not"'; 'introduce it with a complete sentence ended by a colon' for vertical lists.

claim: Page references are avoided as error-prone; sections and sidebars are cited by quoted title and chapters by number.
source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
quote: We avoid page references as much as possible.

verdict.trueWording: We avoid page references as much as possible.
verdict.note: Continues 'They are labor-intensive (they must be added by hand during galley review), and they invite error.' Cross-reference style confirmed: 'When you refer to a chapter, use its number' and 'When you refer to a subsection, including a sidebar, use its title in quotes.' One refinement: a table title is explicitly NOT enclosed in quotes.

claim: Dungeon magazine (Paizo era) required read-aloud text to be a bare-bones area description that never references the viewer or presumes player action, banning phrases like 'you see' and 'as you enter the room'.
source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
quote: it does not make any reference to the viewer

verdict.trueWording: Read-aloud text provides a bare-bones description of the encounter area; it does not make any reference to the viewer.
verdict.note: Verbatim on the page (page 12-13 boundary); my PDF text extractor merely dropped the space at the 'it / does' line break. Next sentence is verbatim too: 'Avoid phrases such as "you see," "as you enter the room," or other phrases that assume any action whatsoever on behalf of the players.' Paizo attribution confirmed by the document itself: byline 'By the DUNGEON Staff', address 'DUNGEON Magazine, Paizo Publishing, 2700 Richards Road, Suite 201, Bellevue, WA'. Era is 3.5e (cites Monster Manual II, Fiend Folio, Draconomicon, DUNGEON #114).

feature: read-aloud text: no creatures, few sentences
claim: Read-aloud text should exclude creatures (whose positions depend on circumstances) and only rarely run more than a few sentences; long descriptive passages belong in player handouts.
source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
quote: should only rarely run more than a few sentences

verdict.trueWording: Read-aloud text for an encounter should only rarely run more than a few sentences.
verdict.note: Both halves verbatim and adjacent: 'You should also avoid including descriptions of any creatures in the room, since their activities and positions in the room often depend on multiple factors (such as if they hear the PCs coming, if it's night or day, and so on).' and 'Long sections of read-aloud text are better served as player handouts.'

claim: The Dungeon house template keys each encounter as header/EL, mandatory Read-Aloud Text first, then General Description, Creature(s), Tactics, Development and Treasure, with adventures of 5,000–15,000 words and about 10,000 preferred.
source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
quote: This section generally precedes the other entries of an encounter

verdict.trueWording: Read-aloud Text, General Description, Creature(s), Tactics, Trap(s), Treasure, Development, and Ad-Hoc XP Adjustment
verdict.note: Quote IS verbatim ('This section generally precedes the other entries of an encounter, although part of the general description might precede it if important to the encounter.'), and the header/EL and word-count halves are confirmed verbatim: 'Each encounter should be rated with an Encounter Level (EL #) in the main encounter header'; sample header '23. Vampire's Den (EL 13)'; 'Our adventures typically range from 5,000 to 15,000 words in length'; 'we automatically reject any adventure manuscript that contains fewer than 5,000 or more than 15,000 words. The ideal manuscript size is 10,000 words.' DOWNGRADED because the claim's section order is wrong: the source order is Treasure BEFORE Development, and the claim omits Trap(s) and Ad-Hoc XP Adjustment from a list it presents as the template. Also 'mandatory Read-Aloud Text' needs care - the heading is labelled (Mandatory) in the template, but the encounters paragraph says 'Each encounter can include any or all of the following sections... Do not include sections that are unnecessary for a given encounter.'

claim: Dungeon guidelines tell writers an adventure is not a short story, to condense backstory in favour of PC involvement, and never to presume PC actions or railroad.
source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
quote: an adventure is not a short story

verdict.trueWording: Regardless of how cool your backstory is, an adventure is not a short story.
verdict.note: Quote verbatim in the query-writing tips. Continues: 'You need to condense or sacrifice background description in favor of telling us about PC involvement. It's how the adventure PLAYS that determines whether or not a proposal is something we want to pick up.' The anti-railroad half is verbatim elsewhere: 'Avoid excessively linear plots that force the story toward an inevitable conclusion or "railroad" the actions of the PCs. The adventure should be flexible enough for PCs to make choices and decisions that could affect the outcome of the story. Avoid rigid timelines.' The design guide adds 'The Adventure Background section should be no more than 5% of the total length of the adventure.'

feature: boxed text length and person (official 5e guidance)
claim: D&D Beyond's official column advises boxed text of roughly four sentences under 100 words, phrased as third-person scene statements rather than 'as you enter, you notice', limited to perceivable sensory detail and excluding PC feelings, villain monologues and non-mechanical game terms.
source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond, 2019-11-06
quote: Read your boxed text aloud to check readability

verdict.trueWording: Tip 5. Read your boxed text aloud to check readability
verdict.note: Quote verbatim (Tip 5 heading). Every element confirmed on the page: 'Four sentences, and less than 100 words.'; third-person example replacing 'As you enter the clearing, you notice the bloated corpse of a headless dragon'; Tip 3 'Describe everything the characters can sense, but not what they can't'; boxed text criticised when it 'assumes a character's feelings, movements, actions, or reactions'; the four-paragraph villain 'boxed-text monologue' criticised; Tip 6 'Avoid game mechanical terms used in a non-mechanical way'. Byline 'by Shawn Merwin / Nov 6, 2019' matches. Fetched by WebFetch and re-fetched raw by curl (HTTP 200).

claim: Boxed text should describe only what characters perceive, treating everything sensed as 'appears to be' rather than asserting hidden facts.
source: Shawn Merwin, D&D Beyond, 2019-11-06
quote: Everything they sense 'appears to be' what it is

verdict.trueWording: Everything they sense “appears to be” what it is.
verdict.note: Word-for-word match; only the inner quotation marks differ (page uses curly double quotes, the claim renders them single). Full context: 'Tip 4. Avoid “seems to be” or “appears to be.” For the characters, perception is reality.' Supports the claim that boxed text should describe only what characters perceive without hedging.

claim: Chris Perkins says published adventure text should entertain the DM who reads it, seeding humour and Easter eggs so the DM is more inclined to run it, and hooks should appeal to 80–90% of players.
source: Todd Kenreck, 'Chris Perkins on Writing Your Own Adventures', D&D Beyond, 2018-04-19
quote: having had a few good laughs

verdict.trueWording: if they come away from reading that adventure, having had a few good laughs, they're much more inclined to run it
verdict.note: Quote verbatim, spoken by Chris Perkins. Also verbatim on the page: 'if you are going to make somebody read something for **** sakes', make it entertaining'; 'Put puns in your adventure. Put little laughs. Put little Easter eggs in your adventure.'; and 'the bait has to be something that is generally applicable ... maybe 80 or 90% of players are going to latch onto'. Byline 'by Todd Kenreck / Apr 19, 2018' matches. Note: the 80-90% line is about the adventure hook/bait, exactly as claimed.

claim: The WotC House Style Guide bundle circulated to freelancers is summarised as: focus on the characters, include a credible threat, focus on the here and now and omit verbose backstories.
source: Mike Shea, 'On Writing Adventures', Sly Flourish, 2019-06-17
quote: Focus on the here and now. Omit verbose backstories.

verdict.trueWording: Focus on the here and now. Omit verbose backstories.
verdict.note: Quote verbatim as one bullet in the article's 'D&D House Style Guide' list. Companion bullets read 'Focus on the importance of the characters.' and 'Include a solid credible threat.' — the claim's shortened wording is a fair summary, not the page's exact words. Framing confirmed: 'This free set of documents from Wizards of the Coast includes the house styles the D&D team gives to freelancers.' Byline 'by Mike on 17 June 2019' matches.

claim: Boxed text is descriptive text in the adventure book meant to be read aloud verbatim or paraphrased, interleaved with rules references, and the DM-facing text explicitly instructs when to read or skip it.
source: Callison-Burch et al., 'Dungeons and Dragons as a Dialogue Challenge for AI', EMNLP 2022, Appendix B
quote: Read the boxed text when you're ready to start.

verdict.trueWording: Read the boxed text when you’re ready to start.
verdict.note: Quote verbatim (curly apostrophe) inside Appendix B, 'B Lost Mine of Phadelver Adventure', of the EMNLP 2022 paper (Callison-Burch, Tomar, Martin, Ippolito et al.). The definition is also verbatim: 'The adventure book provides boxed text, which is descriptive text to be read aloud verbatim or to paraphrase. It also gives details about the combat ... and links to relevant [rules]'; and the skip instruction follows: 'If you create a different adventure hook, skip to the second paragraph'. Paper title is 'Dialog Challenge', not 'Dialogue Challenge' — trivial. Verified by extracting the PDF text locally (15 pages).

claim: McKenzie treats read-aloud text as the adventure's 'at rise' stage direction, typographically set apart and read verbatim, and dates its first appearance to The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan.
source: Brian McKenzie, 'D&D Adventures as Tragedy', Analog Game Studies, 2023-12-18
quote: hints of what may be done are given in this text

verdict.trueWording: Hints of what may be done are given in this text and the DM should only provide vague information if questioned.
verdict.note: Quote verbatim (the article quoting The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan). Confirmed: 'Read-aloud text is analogous to “at rise” descriptions.' and 'D&D adventure writers employ descriptive text in the same way as playwrights use “at rise” descriptions'; 'because it is typically set outside from the other text in a box'; 'the 1980 adventure module The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan marks its first appearance.' One gloss unsupported: the word 'verbatim' never appears in the article — it says the DM 'is instructed to read' the boxed text to players. Byline 'December 18, 2023 Brian McKenzie' matches.

feature: DM preference for boxed text (designer poll)
claim: A Jeremy Crawford Twitter poll cited by McKenzie found 59.5% of DMs prefer occasional boxed text, 34.4% want lots, and about 6% want none.
source: Brian McKenzie, Analog Game Studies, 2023-12-18
quote: occasional boxed text

verdict.trueWording: The results were 59.5% desired “occasional boxed text,” 34.4% “lots of boxed text,” and only 6% of respondents did not want any boxed text.
verdict.note: All three figures and the phrase 'occasional boxed text' verbatim. Attribution confirmed: 'A Twitter poll by D&D's current lead rules designer Jeremy Crawford saw 2,248 replies to the question “How much boxed text (aka read-aloud text) do you like in an adventure you run?”' (endnote 38 cites @JeremyECrawford, 17 Nov 2016). The claim's 'about 6%' matches 'only 6%'.

feature: read-aloud text function and NPC action
claim: Grouling Cover describes module read-aloud text as passages the DM is instructed to read that usually describe location but sometimes narrate NPC action, and likens it to a videogame cut-scene.
source: Jennifer Grouling Cover, The Creation of Narrative in Tabletop Role-Playing Games (McFarland 2010), pp. 64–66, 80
quote: read aloud text that the DM is instructed to read

verdict.trueWording: read aloud text that the DM is instructed to read to the players. Often these passages describe the location, but sometimes they are also used to describe the action of NPCs
verdict.note: Google Books snippet for p.64 of Cover's book carries the quoted fragment word for word plus the location/NPC-action distinction. The cut-scene comparison is on the adjacent snippets: p.65 '... read aloud in the TRPG, but add more visual interest. Cut-scenes are moments in a videogames where the gameplay is interrupted by a visual scene' and p.66 '... read aloud text in the module. The opening of the computer game is a fairly elaborate cut-scene'. Cited pages 64-66 and 80 all return snippets. Route note: WebFetch of the URL returned metadata only; the snippets came from the same URL fetched raw with curl (HTTP 200), whose embedded JSON holds four search_results.

claim: Grouling Cover argues second-person address pulls players directly into the storyworld, situating and immersing them, drawing on Fludernik's narratology of second-person texts.
source: Jennifer Grouling Cover, The Creation of Narrative in Tabletop Role-Playing Games (2010), pp. 21, 85
quote: pulling them directly into the storyworld

verdict.trueWording: second-person, pulling them directly into the storyworld, situating them in a place, and immersing them.
verdict.note: Quote verbatim in the Google Books snippet, together with 'situating' and 'immersing'. Fludernik is confirmed at p.85: 'Monik Fludernik (1994) explains that “second person texts frequently undermine this story-discourse dichotomy by the very nonnaturalness of their design...”'. Caveat: the immersion sentence sits on p.107, not on pp.21/85 as the source field cites; p.21 discusses second person and audience address, p.85 the Fludernik narratology. Same curl route as index 22.

claim: Hines finds Tomb of Annihilation's text repeatedly uses 'tribal', 'exotic' and 'savage', and its Port Nyanzaru read-aloud leans on vague stereotypes (dinosaurs, bright clothing, click languages) rather than specific cultural detail.
source: Mark Hines, Analog Game Studies, 2023-03-19
quote: heavy, characteristic accent

verdict.trueWording: the frequency that words like “tribal,” “exotic,” and “savage” crop up throughout the module
verdict.note: Both halves confirmed. Loaded adjectives verbatim as quoted. Port Nyanzaru: 'the first instance of “flavor text”, or text that the Dungeon Master is explicitly meant to read aloud to the players, highlights dinosaurs, “Minstrels in bright clothing,” and voices speaking “in an unfamiliar language filled with clicks.” Here, we begin to see how the module gestures towards vague stereotypes of the African diaspora'. The claim's quote field ('heavy, characteristic accent') is also verbatim on the page, though it belongs to the DM-guidance sentence (index 25) rather than the Port Nyanzaru passage. Byline 'March 19, 2023 Mark Hines' matches.

claim: Hines notes DM-facing text instructs voicing Chultans with a heavy accent and tongue clicks, and reads background wording like 'correctly ascertain its original purpose' as prose that frames ruins as needing outsider validation.
source: Mark Hines, Analog Game Studies, 2023-03-19
quote: correctly ascertain its original purpose

verdict.trueWording: encouraging players to adopt a certain mentality or approach
verdict.note: First half verified verbatim: 'the game's only guidance in portraying Chultans is to emphasize “tongue clicks” and their “heavy, characteristic accent.”' The quoted fragment 'correctly ascertain its original purpose' is also verbatim. But the claim's characterisation is the claimant's gloss, not Hines's: he presents it as the Archaeologist *background's mechanical feature* (an identity mechanic), arguing it caters to 'dungeons that combine race and place' and is 'meant to evoke images and stereotype in the minds of players' — he never calls it prose and never says ruins need outsider validation. Downgraded for that gap only.

claim: Hewitt shows Curse of Strahd's Death House read-aloud builds gothic atmosphere through decay adjectives (moldy, rusty, gaunt, pale-faced, voluminous) in present-tense third-person description.
source: Meghan Hewitt, Analog Game Studies, 2024-12-15
quote: festooned with moldy skeletons

verdict.trueWording: gothic atmosphere clearly set through the statue and skeletal remains
verdict.note: The Death House passage is quoted verbatim on the page — 'This room is festooned with moldy skeletons that hang from rusty shackles against the walls... a gaunt, pale-faced man wearing a voluminous black cloak' — so all five adjectives are present, and Hewitt does say 'The gothic atmosphere is clearly set through the daunting presence of the statue, as well as the skeletal remains lurking in the corners of the room.' What the article does NOT do is what the claim credits it with: it introduces the passage as 'The suggested description', never uses the terms 'read-aloud' or 'boxed text' (zero occurrences), and makes no argument about decay adjectives, present tense, or third person. The adjective/tense/person analysis is the claimant's, not Hewitt's. Byline 'December 15, 2024 Meghan Hewitt' matches.

claim: Jara analyses rulebooks as framing devices whose covers, prologues, epilogues and embedded fiction shape play; storytelling-game books open with atmospheric prologue fiction, whereas the 1974 D&D booklets used such framing far less.
source: David Jara, 'A Closer Look at the (Rule-) Books', International Journal of Role-Playing 4 (2013)
quote: notoriously less prominent in early TRPGs

verdict.trueWording: “double use” of framing devices was notoriously less prominent in early TRPGs
verdict.note: Quote verbatim in the full-text PDF (journals.uu.se/IJRP/article/download/228/252/576), in the passage 'by observing the simplicity of the original cover of the D&D game from 1974 (See fig. 3), it becomes evident that the aforementioned “double use” of framing devices was notoriously less prominent in early TRPGs'. The storytelling-game prologue point is also explicit: 'practically all of them begin with a prologue consisting of a short narrative text that provides an atmospheric introduction into the fictional setting'. The abstract names 'cover illustrations, prologues and epilogues' as the paratexts studied; section 3.3.2 covers 'Prologues, Epilogues and Framing/Embedded Narratives'. Note: the source's comparison is specifically the covers' double (typographic + pictorial) framing, not framing in general.

claim: Jara coins 'genesic framing' for rulebook text that discloses its own framing and incites players to produce further text, which he says accounts for the medium's persistence.
source: David Jara, IJRP 4 (2013)
quote: what I have called genesic framing

verdict.trueWording: the use of framings in TRPGs to incite the production (and not only the reception) of text is what I have called genesic framing
verdict.note: Quote verbatim, in the conclusion and repeated as a pull-quote. Self-disclosure element confirmed ('of self-disclosure, as well as the use of framings...'), as is the persistence element: 'it is this feature that is likely to account for much of the complexity of the TRPG medium as well as for its persistence in time.' The source hedges with 'likely to account for much of', where the claim says flatly 'accounts for'.

claim: Macdonell argues the 1978 Tomb of Horrors' scripted descriptions and its illustration booklet are dissonant, producing interpretive ambiguity, and that later editions removed the visual assets (abstract only; full text paywalled).
source: Cameron Macdonell, 'Tomes and Tombs', Games and Culture, 2025
quote: visual–textual dissonance produces interpretive ambiguity

verdict.trueWording: the first edition’s visual–textual dissonance produces interpretive ambiguity that might enhance embodied player engagement
verdict.note: ROUTE: journals.sagepub.com returned HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and a browser-UA curl, and the Wayback availability API reports no snapshot for this DOI, so the Sage page itself is unreachable. Verified instead against the publisher-deposited abstract for the same DOI via the Crossref API (HTTP 200): title 'Tomes and Tombs: Toward a Phenomenology of Interiors in Dungeons & Dragons', author Cameron Macdonell, published online 2025-09-03. That abstract carries the claim's quote word for word, and also 'Later editions increasingly removed visual assets'. Unconfirmed at abstract level (full text paywalled, as the claim itself concedes): the year 1978 and the specific 'illustration booklet'; the abstract says 'the first edition' and 'visual assets', and hedges with 'might enhance'.

claim: Monte Cook characterises AD&D's house voice as heavy passive voice, stream-of-consciousness digressions, an advanced vocabulary and an authoritative, treatise-like tone that legitimised the hobby.
source: Monte Cook, 'How you say it', Substack, 2021-07-27
quote: the passive voice a lot, the occasional stream-of-consciousness digressions

verdict.trueWording: using the passive voice a lot, the occasional stream-of-consciousness digressions
verdict.note: Live fetch 200. Quote is word for word in Cook's own sentence, which continues 'an advanced vocabulary (I was a 14-year-old who used terms like "weal or woe" because of Gary), and a very authoritative tone.' The treatise/legitimacy element is also explicit: 'Reading Gary's AD&D Dungeon Master's Guide was like reading a treatise on some vital topic of complexity and depth' and 'it was meaningful to read someone treating the activity we loved as seriously as a scholar would' / 'We felt that it was both validating and compelling.' Claim fully supported.

claim: The community term 'High Gygaxian' (coined by Maliszewski) names Gygax's archaic, thesaurus-driven diction ('perforce', 'antithesis of weal'), long multi-clause sentences and baroque tone, fullest in the 1979 DMG and Vault of the Drow.
source: James Maliszewski, 'High Gygaxian', Grognardia, 2009-02-19

verdict.trueWording: After winning the fight, the characters slept for six hours.

claim: The guide explicitly retires 4e usages: 'save' as 'successful saving throw' and 'result' as 'the number rolled on a die' — 'We have abandoned that practice.'

quote: We have abandoned that practice

verdict.trueWording: In 4E, we used "save" as a synonym for "successful saving throw." We have abandoned that practice.

Minor precision point, not an unsupported limb: the guide attributes the 'result' usage to '3E and 4E', not 4E alone — 'In 3E and 4E, the word "result" was sometimes used as a synonym for "the number rolled on a die."' claim: Write 'deals 10 fire damage', not '10 points of fire damage'; write 'hit point maximum', not 'maximum hit points'; 'magic item' is never 'magical item'.

Page citation pp.6-7 is correct.

claim: Capitalize ability scores, Armor Class, class features, Difficulty Class, feats, languages, planes, skills, racial/monster traits; italicize spell and magic-item names as titles (the spell wall of fire produces a wall of fire).

verdict.trueWording: the wall of fire spell produces a wall of fire

Every listed term is on p.5 'Formatting Game Terms': Terms to Capitalize lists Ability scores, Armor Class, Artifacts, Class features, Difficulty Class, Dungeon Master, Feats, Languages, Planes of existence, Skills, 'Traits in races and monsters'; Terms to Italicize lists Artifacts, Magic items, Spells; and 'The italicized terms are treated as titles, even when they don't use title capitalization.'

claim: Inline subheads (heading 4) end with terminal punctuation, not a colon — 'Keen Senses. You have proficiency…' — and are set in bold italics; bolded stat-block fields are a different thing.
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
quote: followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon

verdict.trueWording: this subhead should be followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon
verdict.note: Quote verbatim on p.2. Limbs: 'The lowest level of our heading hierarchy is the inline subhead. It functions as our heading 4.'; the correct example is verbatim 'Keen Senses. You have proficiency in the Perception skill.' (with the colon version shown as incorrect); and 'Don't confuse an inline subhead with the bolded title of a stat block entry or other data field.' One nuance on the bold-italics limb: it is the guide's fallback instruction, not unconditional — 'If you don't have access to the style, set the subhead in bold italics to distinguish it from text that is simply bold.'

feature: no weeks or months in rules

source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
quote: say a game effect lasts for 7 days

verdict.trueWording: say a game effect lasts for 7 days, not 1 week
verdict.note: Quote verbatim on p.7, section 'Avoid "Week" and "Month"'. Limbs: 'A week is ten days long in the Forgotten Realms, for instance, and is called a tenday.'; 'don't express durations or other lengths of time in weeks or months when you're writing rules'; 'The length of the year varies as well, but you may use years for durations and the like.' One nuance: the guide's stated reason is broader than the claim's — 'The lengths of weeks and months vary in different D&D worlds', with the Realms tenday given as an instance.

claim: The only tone guidance in the guide: D&D is high fantasy about small teams; humor or tragedy is fine if it doesn't overtake the tone, tested against Lord of the Rings / Game of Thrones — 'ring wraiths aren't used for gags'.
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
quote: ring wraiths aren't used for gags

verdict.trueWording: there are moments of humor with the hobbits, but ring wraiths aren't used for gags
verdict.note: Quote verbatim on p.5, section 'High Fantasy'. Limbs verbatim: 'A typical D&D story or adventure is part of the high fantasy subgenre'; 'D&D is about small bands of characters embarking on adventures together'; 'Elements of humor or tragedy are fine, so long as they are true to the facts of the brand and don't overtake the general tone'; 'When in doubt, think about properties like the Lord of the Rings or Game of Thrones.' claim: v1.08a adds a diction rule: avoid 'fellowship' for adventuring groups because D&D companies are 'often fractious or more mercenary'; use group, band, company or especially 'party'.

claim: v1.08a switches from '5th Edition' to lowercase 'fifth edition', preferably as a modifier ('the fifth edition Dungeon Master's Guide').

claim: v1.08a: write 'priest', 'actor', 'god' regardless of gender; '-ess' forms only in in-world titles.
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)
quote: Avoid gender-specific suffixes whenever possible

verdict.trueWording: Avoid gender-specific suffixes whenever possible.

Again, in-world uses of "goddess" are fine.' The '-ess only in in-world titles' limb is very slightly compressed — the guide's condition is 'only if it's part of a person's title or an in-world organizations' titles', i.e. a person's title as well as an organization's. claim: v1.08a requires descending the heading hierarchy without skipping levels, forbids inline subheads used merely for emphasis, and says the best sidebars 'can appear anywhere on a page and still make sense'.

verdict.trueWording: The best sidebars can appear anywhere on a page and still make sense.

For example, do not say "If the player characters open the door, the golem will attack." Instead say, "If the player characters open the door, the golem attacks."' Every limb supported.
